drills.q: Define safe and idempotent precisely, and explain why safety implies idempotency but not the reverse.
drills.a: Safe: no intended server-side side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE). Idempotent: N identical requests leave the server in the same state as 1 (adds PUT, DELETE). Safety implies idempotency because nothing changes, so repeating changes nothing; idempotency doesn't imply safety because PUT/DELETE both change state, just to the same end state regardless of repeat count.

drills.q: Is a repeat DELETE on an already-deleted resource still idempotent if it returns 404 instead of the original 200?
drills.a: Yes -- idempotency is a property of server STATE, not of the HTTP response. 'The resource doesn't exist' is the same state whether it's the first delete (200/204) or a repeat (404); the response is allowed to differ.

drills.q: Why is PUT idempotent but POST is not, reasoning from the actual definitions rather than a memorized table?
drills.a: PUT is defined as 'store this representation as the entire target resource' -- a statement of desired end state, so applying it twice is a no-op the second time by definition. POST is defined as resource-specific processing, canonically 'create a new subordinate resource' -- the spec never claims repetition is a no-op, and creation specifically means each call produces something new.

drills.q: Is PATCH idempotent? Give an example that is and one that isn't.
drills.a: Not by default -- RFC 5789 deliberately doesn't claim it. Depends on the operation encoded in the request: {op: set, field: status, value: shipped} applied twice yields the same result (idempotent in practice); {op: increment, field: counter} applied twice does not (not idempotent). It's a property of the specific patch document, not of the PATCH verb.

drills.q: Design an idempotency-key mechanism for a payment-creation endpoint, including the concurrency edge case.
drills.a: Client generates a UUID per payment attempt, sends it as Idempotency-Key. Server atomically reserves the key (unique constraint or SETNX-equivalent) BEFORE doing any work, executes the charge once, stores (key -> final response); a repeat returns the stored response without re-executing. TTL must exceed the client's maximum retry window including manual replays. Edge case: two retries arriving within milliseconds of each other -- naive read-then-write races and both execute; the reservation step must be atomic and precede the work so the second request sees the key already reserved (409, or brief block) instead of racing past an unenforced check.

drills.q: Explain 401 vs 403 and why conflating them is a real bug, not a style nitpick.
drills.a: 401 = the request lacks valid authentication; correct client behavior is to authenticate/refresh. 403 = authenticated but not authorized; re-authenticating won't help since the problem is permissions, not identity. Conflating them breaks client logic: a client treating every 403 as 'token expired' loops refreshing a token that was never the issue, and one treating every 401 as permanent forbids fails to prompt re-login when it should.

drills.q: Why do 307 and 308 exist when 301 and 302 already redirect?
drills.a: 301/302 predate a strict method-preservation guarantee, and browsers historically rewrote a POST into a GET when following either, dropping the body. 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) explicitly preserve both the original method and body across the redirect -- use these for any redirect that must carry a non-GET method with a payload.

drills.q: Explain how ETags provide both caching and optimistic concurrency using the same mechanism, and whether a weak ETag works for both.
drills.a: Caching: If-None-Match on a GET, matching ETag -> 304 with no body, client reuses its cache. Concurrency: If-Match on a PUT/PATCH, matching ETag -> write proceeds; mismatch -> 412 Precondition Failed, preventing a silent lost update (two clients read the same version, one overwrites the other). A weak ETag (only semantic equivalence) is fine for caching freshness but NOT safe for the concurrency use case, which needs a strong (byte-identical) validator for correct compare-and-swap semantics.

drills.q: A client's request times out. What's the safe retry policy, and why is the timeout genuinely ambiguous?
drills.a: If the method is safe/idempotent (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE), retry with backoff -- worst case you repeat a no-op. If it's POST or an unproven-idempotent PATCH, don't blindly retry; require a client-generated idempotency key or surface the ambiguity to the caller. The timeout is ambiguous because you genuinely don't know if the request was lost or if only the response was lost -- the server may have already fully processed it.

drills.q: Distinguish Cache-Control: no-cache from no-store, and explain why the naming trips people up.
drills.a: no-store: never persist the response anywhere -- for genuinely sensitive data. no-cache: misleadingly named -- it DOES allow storage, but forces revalidation with the origin before every reuse, saving bandwidth on unchanged content but not the round trip. Confusing the two means either over-caching sensitive data or under-caching content that just needed revalidation.

drills.q: A cache serves stale data for 30 seconds after every deploy. Diagnose it, and describe the fix that avoids adding round-trip latency.
drills.a: Likely max-age set too high relative to actual data change frequency, no must-revalidate, and no cache-busting tied to deploys (e.g. ETag computed from something that doesn't reflect the real content change, like a build hash stable across config-only deploys). Fix: shorten max-age, add must-revalidate, and ensure the ETag is derived from actual content state. To avoid adding round-trip latency for the revalidation itself, use stale-while-revalidate=N: serve the stale copy immediately, revalidate in the background, next request gets the fresh copy.

drills.q: Design the conditional-request strategy for a multi-user document-editing API, and explain when a whole-document ETag is the wrong tool.
drills.a: GET returns the document plus a strong ETag; on save, PUT/PATCH sends If-Match with the last-seen ETag. First save succeeds and gets a new ETag; a second concurrent save's If-Match no longer matches -> 412, forcing the client to re-fetch and reapply rather than silently overwriting. Whole-document ETags are too coarse when two users are editing genuinely different, non-conflicting fields of the same document -- that scenario calls for field-level or CRDT/operational-transform merge strategies, not document-wide optimistic concurrency, which is right for rare conflicting writes but wrong for expected frequent concurrent editing of disjoint parts.

drills.q: Why is 429 retryable while most 4xx codes are not, and what should a well-behaved client do differently for it?
drills.a: Most 4xx mean the request itself is malformed or invalid for this resource, so retrying identically fails identically -- pure waste. 429 means the request was valid but rate-limited temporarily. A well-behaved client reads Retry-After and waits exactly that long rather than applying generic exponential backoff or retrying immediately, which would just synchronize retries into the exact storm rate limiting was meant to prevent.

drills.q: An endpoint computes its ETag from the fully-rendered response body. What's wrong with that design, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: It still does all the expensive rendering work before it can decide to return 304, so conditional requests save bandwidth but not the compute cost -- usually the larger of the two for an expensive resource. Fix: derive the ETag from something cheap and representative of the underlying data state (a version column, an updated_at timestamp, a content hash computed and stored at write time) so the conditional check can short-circuit before any expensive rendering happens.

drills.q: Rank GET, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE by how often getting their semantics wrong causes a real production incident, and justify why duplicate charges rank above silent lost updates.
drills.a: 1) POST retried without an idempotency key (duplicate charges/orders) 2) PATCH assumed idempotent by verb alone 3) PUT/PATCH with no If-Match (silent lost updates) 4) 401/403 conflation 5) 301/302 vs 307/308 confusion. Duplicate charges rank above lost updates not because the per-incident severity is worse, but because frequency times blast radius drives incident cost -- every payment retry path is exposed to the duplicate-charge failure mode and it's directly financial, which is how prioritization usually works in practice.
